messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Vulnerability: Being naked, Auditory/Mechanical: Motorcycle noise
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events, Avoid Going Out: Going out, Avoid Exercise: Exercise
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Vinh's Vigil

Vinh Nguyen was forty-six when he came to the clinic, fifteen years after the roadside explosion that ended his first career and began the one that would define the rest of his life. He had been a signals officer with the Army Corps of Engineers in Kandahar Province—steady work, technical work, the kind that suited his methodical mind. On a Tuesday morning in March 2009, his convoy was moving supplies to an outpost when the vehicle ahead of his struck an IED. He remembered the sound first, a crack that seemed to come from everywhere at once, then the smell—acrid, chemical, underneath it something organic and wrong. He had been thrown from his seat, his uniform torn open across his chest and shoulders. For several seconds he lay in the dust unable to move, exposed and certain he would be shot. No one came. The shooting, when it started, came from the ridge line. He crawled behind the wreckage and waited, half-naked in the heat, for four hours until the medevac arrived.

He had not been seriously wounded. The blast had knocked him down; shrapnel had grazed his ribs. The physical injuries healed within weeks. What did not heal was the particular configuration of terror that had crystallized in those hours—the helplessness of exposure, the impossibility of knowing where danger would come from, the way his own senses had become unreliable. He could not see the shooters. He could not predict the next impact. All he could do was wait and listen to the sound of his own breathing and the sporadic gunfire echoing off the rocks.

Vinh returned to the States and left the military. He found work as a software engineer at a mid-sized tech firm in Seattle, married his longtime girlfriend Lena, bought a house in a quiet suburb. For the first few years, the symptoms were manageable—bad dreams, some hypervigilance, the occasional moment of panic when a car backfired. But over the past decade, something had shifted. The vigilance had not diminished; it had metastasized.

Now, at home in the evenings, Vinh found himself unable to truly relax. Even with the doors locked and the curtains drawn, he was alert—listening for sounds that did not belong, tracking the position of windows, mentally cataloguing exits. When a motorcycle roared past on the street outside, his heart rate spiked and his hands went cold. The sound was too much like the gunfire, too sudden, too loud. He would sit rigid until the noise faded, his mind flooded with the sensory memory of that morning: not just the sound of shots, but the specific pitch and rhythm of them, the way they had seemed to come from nowhere.

He had begun avoiding things in ways that felt logical at the time but had accumulated into a kind of confinement. He stopped going out unless absolutely necessary—the unpredictability of unfamiliar places terrified him. He could not assess the danger in a new restaurant or a shopping center, could not predict where a threat might emerge. He stopped watching television, stopped reading the news, because anything that touched on conflict or violence would trigger the film that played in his head—not a coherent narrative but a sensory loop: the smell, the sound of his own breathing, the vulnerability of his exposed skin, the crack of the blast, over and over. He could not put it into words, which made it worse. When Lena asked him what he was thinking about, what was wrong, he had no way to explain that his mind was not thinking in language but in sensation and dread.

Exercise had become impossible. Going to the gym meant being around strangers in close quarters, meant being vulnerable in a changing room. Even walking on his own street made him tense. Strangers approaching him—the mailman, a neighbor—triggered a surge of threat detection that he knew was irrational but could not override.

What finally brought him to seek help was not a crisis but a quiet realization. His company had asked him to work in the office three days a week instead of remote. The thought of sitting in an open plan with colleagues, of being unable to control who approached him or when, of being trapped in a space he could not fully assess, had triggered such intense dread that he had called in sick for a week. Lena had found him in the basement, sitting in the dark, unable to articulate why. She had insisted he see someone. He was afraid that if he left the house, if he opened himself to the world again, something terrible would happen. But he was also afraid of what would happen if he stayed here, locked in the vigilance, waiting for a danger that had already passed.
